name: Raw eggs / oysters / zinc-rich foods
lead: Raw eggs, oysters and other zinc-rich foods are eaten by some people as part of a diet aimed at supporting testosterone and, through it, a leaner, more muscular and more masculine physique. The reasoning rests mainly on zinc, a mineral the body needs to produce testosterone, and on the long bodybuilding tradition of eating large quantities of eggs and shellfish for muscle gain [1][2][14].

Reference texts report that zinc deficiency can lower circulating testosterone, and that supplementing zinc beyond adequate intake does not change serum levels [1][2]. Oysters are described as by far the richest dietary source of zinc [2]. Eggs, raw or cooked, are valued by lifters mainly as an inexpensive protein and choline source rather than as a zinc source.

On looksmax.org, raw eggs are a recurring topic: members post about drinking a dozen or more at a time, ask about taste and safety, and argue over whether raw eggs offer anything cooked eggs do not [9][10][11][13]. Food-safety reviews describe infection risks linked to raw shellfish and raw eggs, which is part of how experts discuss the practice [4][5][3].

chain: Zinc-rich foods supply a mineral needed for testosterone production
Adequate zinc supports normal testosterone, which supports training adaptation
angle.text: Followers of the practice eat oysters, eggs and other zinc-rich foods to keep zinc intake high so testosterone production is not limited, with the aim of building muscle and a more masculine physique. Reference texts describe a testosterone effect where zinc was lacking to begin with.

Testosterone falls with zinc deficiency; extra zinc beyond adequacy does not change serum levels [1][2]

paras: Zinc is required to produce testosterone, and deficiency can reduce levels, potentially leading to hypogonadism and delayed puberty [2]. A 1963 case report described a young man whose stunted growth and underdeveloped genitalia reversed with zinc supplementation [2]. The testosterone article similarly says zinc deficiency lowers testosterone, while over-supplementation does not change serum levels [1].

A 3-ounce serving of fried oysters is reported to contain about 74 mg of zinc, compared with about 7 mg in the same amount of braised beef chuck; other sources include crab, beef, cashews, lobster, pork and almonds [2]. Phytates in whole grains can reduce zinc absorption [2].
Eggs are a source of protein and choline. Wikipedia's egg article lists about 294 mg of choline per 100 g of hard-boiled whole egg [3].

Eating raw eggs is associated in popular culture with strength athletes; a forum poster recalls bodybuilding coach Vince Gironda promoting a high-egg diet, with raw eggs, on the premise that eggs supply what the body needs for hormones and gains [14]. Looksmax.org threads show members drinking or blending raw eggs in quantities of a dozen or more, sometimes with milk [12][13][11].

Some members argue that raw eggs are not worth the trouble, noting less protein per egg and the convenience of cooking; others say raw eggs are simply easier to add to a shake [10]. One poster argues the main reason to choose raw is choline content [10]. Wikipedia reports that raw egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable versus about 91 percent for cooked egg, and that health authorities advise against raw egg consumption for people susceptible to salmonellosis [3]. A 2022 randomized trial in the Journal of Nutrition examined raw eggs for postexercise recovery in healthy young men [8].

Reviews note that infections from Vibrio bacteria, which live in marine environments, most often follow shellfish consumption, especially oysters, and that such infections are increasing in the United States [4]. A 2022 review describes filter-feeding molluscs as able to accumulate pathogenic microorganisms, with outbreaks reported more often as consumption has risen [5]. Mollusc allergy, driven mainly by the muscle protein tropomyosin, is also documented [6].
A controlled feeding study in 18 men found oyster, clam, crab and mussel diets lowered some blood lipids when eaten with moderate fat restriction [7].

No studies found testing raw eggs, oysters or zinc-rich foods as a testosterone or physique intervention in men with normal zinc status. Related research includes work on zinc deficiency and testosterone summarised in reference texts [1][2], a 2022 randomized trial on raw eggs and postexercise recovery in healthy young men [8], and a 1990 controlled trial of shellfish diets and blood lipids in 18 men [7].

timeline.event: A case report describes reversal of stunted growth and underdeveloped genitalia in a young man after zinc supplementation [2].
A controlled trial reports blood-lipid changes in men fed oyster, clam, crab and mussel diets [7].
Journal of Nutrition publishes a randomized trial on raw eggs and postexercise recovery in healthy young men [8].

lore.intro: Raw eggs appear on looksmax.org as a cheap high-protein, high-choline habit, with threads from members drinking large numbers at once and others asking whether it is safe or worthwhile [9][10][11][13]. Oysters are discussed as a zinc source for testosterone.

claims.claim: Drinking raw eggs is a cheap way to eat a lot of protein and choline
claims.believers: Members describe blending or drinking a dozen or more raw eggs for convenience, and one poster says raw eggs are the best choline source [10][11][13].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports raw egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable versus about 91 percent cooked, and that health authorities advise against raw eggs for susceptible groups because of Salmonella [3].

claims.claim: Eggs supply what the body needs for hormones and gains
claims.believers: A T Nation poster recalls Vince Gironda pitching a very high daily egg intake, raw, on the premise that eggs contain the nutrients to get hormones right for gaining [14].
claims.experts: Reference texts link testosterone to zinc status rather than egg intake, and say supplementation beyond adequacy does not raise serum testosterone [1][2].

claims.claim: Oysters and other zinc-rich foods raise testosterone
claims.believers: Proponents point to zinc's role in testosterone production and oysters' very high zinc content [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports deficiency lowers testosterone but zinc supplementation above adequacy has no effect on serum levels [1][2].

claims.claim: Raw eggs are no better than cooked
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster calls raw eggs less nutritious, less tasty and not worth skipping the cooking, citing studies supporting cooked eggs [10].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports higher protein bioavailability for cooked egg [3].

card.summary: Oysters and eggs for testosterone via zinc; deficiency lowers T, but extra zinc is reported not to raise it further.
card.note: Raw animal foods carry general food-safety considerations not covered in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Some people eat oysters, raw eggs and other zinc-rich foods hoping to raise testosterone.

Reference texts say zinc is needed to make testosterone and deficiency lowers it, but that extra zinc beyond adequacy does not change serum levels.
quick.mechanism: Zinc is required for testosterone production, so correcting a shortfall may restore levels [2]. Oysters are an unusually zinc-dense food [2].
quick.risks: The sources reviewed describe no harms from zinc-rich foods. Raw eggs and raw shellfish are not addressed in them.
